title: Flinders Medical Centre Study Abroad Report
paragraphs: I did a 12-week clinical clerkship at Flinders Medical Centre (FMC), the hospital attached to Flinders University, in Adelaide, the capital of South Australia, Australia. I will report on the city of Adelaide and FMC, the state of my clerkship, and what life there was like.

First, I will introduce the town of Adelaide. It is a city of about one million people, compact and very livable: thirty minutes by car to the west takes you to beautiful beaches, and thirty minutes to the east to hills rich in nature. People who immigrated from various countries live there, the people are kind, and public safety is very good.

FMC is located in the south of Adelaide and is one of the largest hospitals in Adelaide. It has about 600 beds. I did a 12-week clerkship in the emergency department (ED). 74,000 patients visit the ED at FMC each year. The facilities were large and there were many doctors, and my impression was that it is more developed than EDs in Japan. There were about 60 emergency doctors in total, working in a three-shift system. Handovers were properly carried out at the shift changes, and my impression was that the doctors' working conditions were well maintained. In addition, every week there was a teaching seminar on each day of the week, and many study sessions were held to improve the quality of medical care daily, such as sharing interesting cases experienced in the daily ED and doing simulation training using models. I felt that the teaching system was well established.

This is about my clerkship. For the first three weeks I did the clerkship in a shadowing format, following specific doctors, starting by getting used to how the ED works and to the people. For the remaining nine weeks, I did the clerkship in three areas, three weeks each. I mainly took the history and examined patients by myself and consulted the doctor. After that, we examined together and I received feedback. If there was a procedure, I was actually allowed to do it under the doctor's guidance. For example, peripheral lines and sutures. If there was an opportunity, I was also allowed to do arterial blood gases and urinary catheters.

The doctors were very kind, tried hard to listen to and understand my clumsy English, and explained things in a way that I could understand. Not only that, they spoke to me every time we met, and after working together they always said, "Thanks for your help." They treated me not as a student but as a member of the team working together, and thanks to that I was able to take part actively and gain confidence.

The atmosphere of the ED at FMC was very good. Even outside the workplace, about once a month the ED members (doctors, nurses and other staff) held parties (I too was allowed to take part once). Not only doctors among themselves but nurses and doctors too called each other by name, and I felt that each person is recognized as a member of the team.

Through the clerkship I also met a doctor whom I thought I should aim to become in the future. That doctor was extremely gentlemanly toward patients and staff alike, spoke at the same eye level, and was always thinking and acting about what was best for the patient. I think I learned from him the core of what it takes to work as a doctor.

Life there was also very fulfilling. I shared a house with two local boys. Both were very kind and talked to me a lot, always invited me to come along whenever they went to a party or event, and took me to various places. Thanks to them my English improved, I came to know Adelaide well, and I came to know their values and ways of thinking. The time I spent with them will be an unforgettable memory for life.

In fact, just before going abroad, I was very anxious about studying abroad. My English ability was not at a good level, and I thought even my medical knowledge might be insufficient. Even so, I was helped by the local people and was able to learn many things, and this study abroad was without a doubt an experience that will influence my life from now on. Finally, I would like to take this opportunity to thank Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川 and everyone at the International Collaboration Office, the people I met in Adelaide, and my family and friends. Thank you very much.
